abstract: Morphogenesis is the emergence of structured form. As with cells during embryo development, social insects may follow similar developmental principles when constructing their nest. Here, we present the first four-dimensional (4D) "atlas" of honeybee nest development at per-cell resolution. Colonies showed specialization at the cell and comb scales, analogous to the differentiation of cell types and tissues in embryos. Across colonies, nests had consistent patterns of organization that varied seasonally: cell contents were clustered and stratified with pollen accumulating on one side of the nest and nectar on the other. The directionality of this protein-carbohydrate polarization was reliably predicted by nest initiation point. By the season's end, nests had undergone an organizational metamorphosis, from asymmetrical polarization to a centralized layout. To test the functional importance of this sequenced organization, we experimentally manipulated nest architecture in a subset of colonies (n = 6 of 12) by weekly shuffling the order and orientation of all combs. Shuffled colonies changed what their cells contained more frequently, had more uniform comb-level organization, and lost their nest-level organization but maintained colony-level performance in key metrics (nest contents, worker population, and nest size). Autoregressive modeling showed that intact three-dimensional structure was necessary to accurately predict cell contents from spatial context, and this predictability collapsed under shuffling, suggesting informational benefits of intact architecture. This work shows how developmental principles apply beyond the organismal form to the extended phenotype, offering resilience in collective systems.
